studies.Screening Record ID: 41761190|Plant protein intake|Kidney and renal pelvis cancer
studies.Population: Adults aged 37–73 years in the UK Biobank
studies.Smoking Status: Never, previous, or current smoker; adjusted for smoking status
studies.Ethnicity Basis: NA: no field-specific ethnicity evidence was available
studies.Reference: The association between plant protein intake and cancer risk: a prospective cohort study.
studies.Authors: Hu S, Yang R, Deng Y, Xue D, Sun Y, Xiao X, Shen Z, Wang Y, Wu Q, Wu J, Dai Z
studies.comparison_type: Highest quartile (Q4) versus lowest quartile (Q1) of plant protein intake
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: Plant protein consumption information was assessed using validated 24-hour dietary recalls.

sample_size.excerpt: This prospective cohort study included 192,428 participants from the UK Biobank, recruited from 2006 and followed until 2023.

cases.location: Results, Characteristics of study population; Table 1

effect_size.excerpt: Compared to participants in the lowest quartile of plant protein intake, those in the highest quartile had HRs for overall cancer, lung cancer, renal cancer, and colorectal cancer of 0.91 (95% CI = 0.88-0.95, P < 0.001), 0.86 (95% CI = 0.73-1.00, P = 0.048), 0.69 (95% CI = 0.55-0.87, P = 0.002), and 0.89 (95% CI = 0.79-1.00, P = 0.046), respectively. Furthermore, each 10% increase in the ratio of plant protein to total daily protein was associated with a 3% lower overall cancer risk (HR = 0.97, 95% CI = 0.95-0.98, P < 0.001).
